routes.description: Establish Christian theism as more reasonable than skeptical atheism through a cumulative case from cosmic origins, fine-tuning, objective morality, Jesus' resurrection, and direct religious experience, while addressing proposed defeaters.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the principal evidential strands jointly support a personal, morally perfect creator and the Christian identification of that creator more strongly than the skeptical alternatives undermine those inferences.

motionBridge.description: The combined evidence must make Christian theism more reasonable than skeptical atheism.

centralBridges.description: A beginning of the universe and an applicable causal principle must support a transcendent personal creator.
Life-permitting fine-tuning must favor intelligent design over necessity, chance, or selection-based alternatives.
Objective moral values and duties must require and receive an adequate foundation in God.
Resurrection evidence and religious experience must connect generic theism to the Christian-God hypothesis.

subsidiaryBridges.description: The evidential strands must be assessed cumulatively under a burden that also requires justification for skeptical atheism.
Objections from evil, hiddenness, religious diversity, and naturalistic epistemology must not defeat the cumulative inference.

routes.description: Show that the specific Christian-God hypothesis lacks sufficient evidential support because its main arguments rely on disputed premises, exceed their conclusions, face natural alternatives, and conflict with evil and hiddenness.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the affirmative evidence does not adequately distinguish Christian theism from rival explanations and the observed world supplies material counterevidence to the claimed divine attributes.

motionBridge.description: The evidence must fail to make Christian theism more reasonable than skeptical atheism.

centralBridges.description: Neither an absolute cosmic beginning nor a causal inference to an immaterial personal creator must be treated as established.
Fine-tuning and morality must admit alternatives that prevent their use as distinctive evidence for the Christian God.
Resurrection reports and religious experience must lack the reliability needed to distinguish Christianity from natural or rival religious accounts.
Evil, suffering, and sincere nonbelief must count against a perfectly good, omnipotent, relational God.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Christian theism must bear an appropriately demanding burden as one specific supernatural hypothesis among incompatible alternatives.
Any limited anomaly or unexplained cause must not be extended beyond the evidence to the full divine attributes.

sections.title: Burden, Religious Diversity, and Epistemic Method
sections.rationale: This issue governs how the specific Christian hypothesis is compared with skeptical atheism, rival religions, experiential claims, rational intuition, and empirically grounded inquiry.

sections.title: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator
sections.rationale: This issue contains the principal inference from the universe's alleged beginning through causal premises to a timeless, immaterial, personal cause.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning, Design, and Alternative Explanations
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether life-permitting conditions favor intelligent design and whether that inference reaches the kind of God specified by the motion.

sections.title: Objective Morality and Divine Grounding
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether objective value and obligation exist, whether non-theistic accounts can ground them, and whether a divine lawgiver is required.

sections.title: Resurrection Evidence and Religious Experience
sections.rationale: This issue bears directly on the transition from generic theism to Christianity through historical claims about Jesus and purported immediate awareness of God.

sections.title: Evil, Suffering, and Divine Hiddenness
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether suffering and sincere nonbelief conflict with the claimed divine attributes and whether the proposed theistic purposes answer that conflict.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The universe began to exist and therefore has an uncaused, timeless, immaterial, personal cause beyond space and time.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly introduces Craig, and the uninterrupted opening address presents this as his first argument.

response.rationale: Constructive cosmological case supplying the beginning, causal conclusion, and proposed attributes of the cause; it has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: A developed constructive move that explicitly states its premises and principal conclusion.

precisionFindings.rationale: The syllogistic core is recoverable, but the transition from transcendent cause to a personal being compresses several attribute and scope distinctions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The immediate syllogistic conclusion is presented as necessary, while the further personal-cause attributes receive less warrant than that force suggests.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The causal syllogism is clear, but a material bridge remains from a transcendent cause to an immaterial personal agent.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt gives reasons for several causal attributes but compresses support for the universe's beginning and for personality.

relevanceBurden.rationale: This directly supplies the indispensable cosmological-creator bridge and ranks near the top of that central tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The selected span primarily advances the affirmative inference rather than evaluating a developed opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly infers a transcendent cause and describes it as uncaused, changeless, timeless, immaterial, and ultimately personal.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The universe's narrowly life-permitting constants and initial conditions are better explained by intelligent design than by physical necessity or chance.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig labels this as his second argument during the same uninterrupted opening presentation.

response.rationale: Constructive design inference comparing physical necessity, chance, and design as explanations of life-permitting cosmic conditions; no reply target applies.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The move gives a clear explanatory comparison, though the chance analysis is compressed in the selected evidence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The explanatory claim is clear, but the asserted three-option scope and relevant probability space retain an implicit qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Design is strongly favored after a compressed trilemma whose exhaustiveness and probability assumptions are not fully defended here.

charity.alternative: Fine-tuning may arise through physical necessity or chance rather than design.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those alternatives require defensible laws, probability measures, or selection mechanisms before comparative likelihoods can be fixed.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The abductive structure is usable, but the exhaustiveness of necessity, chance, and design is a material implicit bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Narrow life-permitting ranges and independence from laws are invoked, but probability measures and rival mechanisms remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central requirement that fine-tuning favor design over necessity and chance.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move identifies the principal alternatives but handles their strongest probabilistic and selection-based qualifications only briefly.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly lists necessity, chance, and design and argues that constants and quantities are independent of physical laws.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Objective moral values and duties exist, and their validity and binding force require God as an adequate foundation.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly announces a third argument and develops both premises and its conclusion in his opening speech.

response.rationale: Constructive moral argument stating that objective moral values and duties exist only if God exists; it has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The move clearly states its conditional and definition, though its grounding warrant remains substantially compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: Objective values are defined as valid and binding, but the exact dependence relation between those values and God is left implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical dependence claim exceeds the selected support because competing realist grounds and the value-duty distinction are not resolved.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument form is clear, but the decisive bridge from objective normativity to divine foundation remains underargued.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The definition is supplied, yet the existence premise and exclusive divine-grounding premise rely mainly on assertion in this span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supplies the central moral-ground bridge and is highly relevant within that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: This opening formulation does not yet engage a sufficiently developed non-theistic grounding alternative for a charity test.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig defines objective values as valid and binding and states the conditional that without God objective moral values and duties would not exist.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Jesus' empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and the disciples' resulting belief are best explained by his resurrection, which entails God's existence.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig identifies this as his fourth argument and presents it continuously as part of his enumerated opening case.

response.rationale: Constructive historical inference from an empty tomb, appearances, and resulting belief to resurrection and hence divine action; no reply target applies.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The move provides a structured three-fact case, although historical verification and rival comparison are compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The three asserted facts and conclusion are recoverable, but historian consensus and best-explanation scope need bounded qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The phrase 'I believe' supplies some qualification, but the strong historical conclusion outruns the limited source and rival analysis shown.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The abductive inference is coherent, but a material bridge remains from the reported facts to resurrection as uniquely best explanation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific historical claims and an appeal to majority recognition are supplied, while source independence and alternative comparison remain limited.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly addresses the central Christian-identification bridge through the resurrection claim.

representationalCharity.rationale: The opening case states its preferred explanation without developing a specific naturalistic rival strongly enough for testing.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies three facts said to be widely recognized and begins with the empty-tomb claim as evidence best explained by resurrection.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: A person can know that God exists through immediate personal experience independently of propositional arguments.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly introduces this as his fifth consideration in the uninterrupted conclusion of his opening case.

response.rationale: Constructive epistemic claim that immediate experience can yield knowledge of God independently of argument; there is no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The proposition is clear, but the selected support chiefly describes claimed experience rather than establishing its reliability.

precisionFindings.rationale: Immediate experience is intelligible, but 'know' and the class of persons entitled to the claim are not fully stabilized.

calibrationFindings.rationale: As a possibility claim its force is restrained, though its epistemic entitlement still requires a reliability or defeater condition.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between inferential and immediate knowledge is coherent, but the reliability bridge remains materially implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Biblical examples and Hick's description illustrate the claim but do not establish that the experience reliably tracks God.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially supports the subsidiary cumulative-method bridge, but does not by itself establish the public comparative motion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The span presents a first-person epistemic route and does not evaluate a developed competing account of such experiences.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly says this is not an argument and claims knowledge wholly apart from argument through immediate experience of God.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Conflicting religions produced through human cognitive tendencies and cultural transmission show that common religious belief-forming methods are unreliable guides to truth.
moves.attributionBasis: Millican delivers the entire passage continuously in his opening address and expressly distinguishes it from a genetic fallacy.

response.rationale: Constructive epistemic objection arguing that incompatible outputs undermine the reliability of common religious belief-forming methods; no target applies.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The move supplies a clear reliability argument using incompatible exclusive religious claims.

precisionFindings.rationale: The incompatibility claim is clear, but 'method' aggregates potentially different traditions and mechanisms under an implicit scope condition.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Diversity supports caution, but incompatibility alone does not show that every relevant belief-forming method is generally unreliable.

charity.alternative: One exclusive religion may be true despite widespread religious disagreement.
charity.decisiveQualification: The objection concerns the reliability of shared or similar methods, not the bare logical possibility that one tradition is correct.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from conflicting outputs to reduced method reliability is coherent, though method individuation remains a material ambiguity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete incompatible religions are identified, but the causal and methodological similarity among their belief processes is only compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: This centrally supports the history-and-experience reliability burden by challenging religious methods as truth guides.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move explicitly allows that at most one exclusive religion could be true while preserving its reliability challenge.

moves.evidenceBasis: Millican cites incompatible Judaism, Christianity, and Islam and argues that a method yielding conflicting beliefs cannot simply be relied upon.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Because Christianity is one specific hypothesis among numerous incompatible religions and disembodied minds lack solid evidence, it requires an exceptionally strong evidential case.
moves.attributionBasis: Millican states the burden conclusion in his own opening speech and supports it through a continuous comparison with rival hypotheses.

components.text: Whether immediate religious experience can justify the specific Christian-God hypothesis despite incompatible religious claims.
Whether the evidence specifically identifies the Christian God rather than one among many incompatible supernatural hypotheses.

response.rationale: The move contacts the specific-identification demand by insisting that Christianity compete with many incompatible hypotheses, though its numerical probability allocation is not established.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive specificity issue but only partially answers the separate reliability and evidential merits of each affirmative route.

precisionFindings.rationale: The burden claim is clear, but 'thousands,' the fifty-percent allocation, and 'overwhelmingly strong' lack stable methodological definitions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A strong comparative burden is defensible, but equal or shared prior probability across unspecified religions is not warranted here.

charity.alternative: Christianity may receive distinctive evidence rather than an equal prior share among all religions.
charity.decisiveQualification: Distinctive evidence can alter priors, so diversity establishes a comparative burden but not the stated numerical allocation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative-burden point is coherent, but the probability division and move from agnosticism toward atheism contain substantial unsupported bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Religious plurality is relevant evidence, while the asserted priors and exceptional burden level receive little independent support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supplies the subsidiary specific-hypothesis burden and ranks strongly within that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes the need for evidence but materially weakens the affirmative alternative through an unsupported probability-sharing picture.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts the specific Christian claim with thousands of conflicting religions and demands an overwhelmingly strong affirmative case.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Neither the beginning of the local universe nor the Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem establishes that the global physical universe had an absolute beginning.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted first-person rebuttal remains within Millican's identified speech and directly addresses Craig by name.

components.text: Whether evidence for a local cosmic beginning establishes an absolute beginning of the global physical universe.
Whether the Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem rules out a globally past-eternal physical reality.

response.rationale: The reply directly distinguishes the local universe from a possible global universe and contests the theorem's reach, contacting the beginning premise decisively.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive cosmic-beginning premise and identifies the local-to-global inference gap.

precisionFindings.rationale: The local/global distinction and limited theorem conclusion are stated in clear, stable, explicitly qualified terms.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The reply argues underdetermination rather than certainty and appropriately confines its claim to what the cited considerations fail to establish.

charity.alternative: Cosmological evidence may establish an absolute beginning through philosophical and physical arguments taken together.
charity.decisiveQualification: A local beginning and average expansion condition do not alone entail a boundary for every global physical model.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between local and global beginnings directly defeats an illicit entailment, with only detailed model conditions left compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The theorem and philosophical-infinity route are specifically identified, though technical cosmological documentation is not developed in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The reply directly attacks the indispensable cosmological-creator bridge at its beginning premise.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply identifies Craig's two standard routes and preserves their combined relevance while contesting their global entailment.

moves.evidenceBasis: Millican states that a local beginning permits a cause within a global universe and that a globally infinite past is not thereby contradictory.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Even if the physical universe had a nonphysical cause, identifying it as an immaterial personal mind exceeds both the available evidence and human cognitive competence.
moves.attributionBasis: Millican explicitly introduces Craig's further inference and develops the objection continuously in his own speech.

components.text: Whether a nonphysical cause of the physical universe may validly be identified as an immaterial personal mind.

response.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses the missing evidence for substrate-free minds and states that the personal-mind identification is speculation beyond the causal conclusion.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly targets the decisive attribute inference and states the defeating consequence for the personal-cause conclusion.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional concession and narrower objection to identifying the cause as a mind are clearly separated and recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The inference-gap diagnosis is well calibrated, but 'no evidence whatever' is stronger than the selected support can establish.

charity.alternative: A timeless cause may need personal agency to originate a temporal effect without antecedent determining conditions.
charity.decisiveQualification: That conceptual proposal does not itself supply empirical evidence that minds can exist without any physical substrate.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reply correctly separates a nonphysical cause from a personal mind and identifies the missing entailment with a bounded omission.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The absence of established substrate-free minds supports caution, though the universal negative and competence claim remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: This directly attacks the central bridge from cosmic causation to a personal creator.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly grants a nonphysical cause conditionally but omits the strongest agency-based rationale for personality.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt conditionally grants a physical-universe cause but emphasizes the absence of evidence for minds existing without a physical substrate.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: A moral argument for God must precisely define the relevant sense of objective value and establish both that such values exist and that they require God.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly identifies Craig's moral argument, quotes its definition, and closes his speech by presenting a direct challenge.

components.text: Whether objective morality is defined consistently and whether both its existence and dependence on God are established.

response.rationale: The reply justifies replacing the bare conditional with two necessary evidential demands: define the relevant objectivity and prove both existence and divine dependence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly preserves the moral argument's legitimate issue while identifying the two propositions that require support.

precisionFindings.rationale: The demanded definition, existence proof, and divine-dependence proof are distinctly and stably formulated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker expresses doubt but leaves the challenge open pending the affirmative answer, matching the limited argumentative posture.

charity.alternative: Objective moral values may be intuitively evident and best grounded in God.
charity.decisiveQualification: The same sense of objectivity must be maintained across both the existence premise and the grounding inference.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The two-part burden follows directly from the affirmative moral syllogism and exposes its decisive definitional and grounding requirements.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The reply is chiefly diagnostic and needs limited external evidence; its demands track the stated affirmative premises closely.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central moral-ground bridge by isolating both indispensable premises.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately identifies the affirmative structure and demands support without assuming in advance that no answer is possible.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks for a precise sense of objective morality requiring God and solid evidence for objective values in that same sense.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: A negative answer to whether God exists requires justification rather than receiving default status, and the case for theism may draw on logic, evidence, and experience.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Craig, after which Craig recapitulates his two contentions and directly answers Millican's opening objections.

components.text: Whether only the affirmative bears a burden and whether an unsupported negative answer should receive default status.

response.rationale: The reply directly contests a one-sided burden and distinguishes unsupported atheism from agnosticism, though it does not erase the affirmative's specific-hypothesis burden.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the burden-allocation demand explicitly but supplies only a partial account of comparative evidential burdens.

precisionFindings.rationale: The atheism-versus-agnosticism distinction is clear, but the debate question does not itself specify symmetrical evidential thresholds.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A defended negative assertion bears a burden, but this does not establish equal burdens or remove the burden on a specific positive hypothesis.

charity.alternative: The affirmative claimant bears the principal burden while nonbelief may remain a default withholding position.
charity.decisiveQualification: An explicit claim that God does not exist differs from mere suspension of belief and requires some justification.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between atheistic assertion and agnostic suspension is coherent, with a bounded ambiguity about debate-wide burden symmetry.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The claim is primarily methodological and well explained, though no general burden principle is independently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially attacks the subsidiary specific-hypothesis burden's one-sided formulation but does not complete the cumulative motion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly preserves agnosticism as a default while challenging only an asserted negative conclusion.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig says that answering the debate question negatively requires justification and otherwise leaves agnosticism as the default position.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Something cannot begin without either a material or an efficient cause, and events in a structured quantum vacuum are not counterexamples to that causal principle.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig directly attributes the contrary objections to Millican and answers them continuously with causal distinctions, quantum physics, and metaphysical reasoning.

components.text: Whether observed quantum events or the absence of a material cause defeat the efficient-causal principle.

response.rationale: The reply distinguishes material from efficient causes and expressly explains why events in a structured quantum setting are not beginnings from nothing.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the causal counterexample directly, though it does not answer the separate local-to-global beginning objection.

precisionFindings.rationale: Material and efficient causes are clearly distinguished, but the universal scope of the causal principle remains implicitly qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conceptual distinction is strong, while 'doubly impossible' states more modal force than the selected defense establishes.

charity.alternative: Quantum events may occur without deterministic antecedent causes and challenge a universal causal premise.
charity.decisiveQualification: A quantum vacuum is a structured physical state and is not equivalent to absolute nothingness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The material/efficient-cause distinction coherently blocks the proposed counterexample, with universal applicability still a bounded bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual analysis is specific, but the empirical characterization of all relevant quantum events is not documented here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central causal requirement while answering a proposed counterexample to efficient causation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply addresses the strongest relevant quantum-vacuum reading while preserving the distinction between determinism and efficient causation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes material from efficient causation and argues that lacking both would not be less problematic than lacking only material causation.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Naturalistic ethical systems do not adequately ground intrinsic human value or binding duties, whereas moral prescriptions are plausibly grounded in a divine lawgiver.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig marks the transition to the moral argument and directly evaluates the secular ethical theories Millican had previously offered.

components.text: Whether binding moral duties can be intelligibly grounded without a prescriber or moral lawgiver.
Whether non-theistic accounts can ground intrinsic human value as distinct from obligation.

response.rationale: The reply directly addresses divine dependence for obligations through the prescription-prescriber analogy but does not establish objective values or fully answer non-theistic realism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive grounding component while leaving the existence premise and rival realist accounts substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The lawgiver thesis is clear, but 'prescription' risks shifting between linguistic commands and categorical normative reasons.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The analogy makes divine grounding plausible to the speaker but does not exclude impersonal accounts of categorical normative reasons.

charity.alternative: Objective obligations may be irreducible normative facts or grounded in reasons rather than commands.
charity.decisiveQualification: Calling obligations prescriptions does not by itself establish that every binding reason is issued by a personal prescriber.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The prescription-prescriber argument is intelligible but depends on a substantial equivocation between grammatical prescriptions and normative obligations.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Appeal to what ethicists recognize and the lawgiver analogy supplies limited support without serious rival comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The reply directly addresses the central divine-grounding requirement for moral obligation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply asserts that rival grounding is unintelligible without addressing the strongest non-command realist alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig argues that prescriptions require prescribers and therefore that moral prescriptions require a moral lawgiver to become intelligible obligations.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Fine-tuning supplies at most a cautious design consideration and does not establish the morally perfect, omnipotent Christian God rather than natural alternatives or rival designers.
moves.attributionBasis: Following his introduction by the moderator, Millican explicitly begins his fine-tuning response and sustains it until announcing a new topic.

components.text: Whether fine-tuning distinguishes an omniperfect Christian God from natural alternatives or rival designers.
Whether current probability and physical assumptions warrant a strong design inference.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges both the evidential force of current physics and the inference from some designer to the morally perfect Christian God.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the strongest identification and underdetermination components of the design inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The modest-support conclusion and the gap between a designer and the Christian God are clearly and explicitly bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move concedes that fine-tuning may count as a cautious consideration while denying that it establishes the specified divine attributes.

charity.alternative: Fine-tuning can raise the probability of theism even if it does not deductively prove every divine attribute.
charity.decisiveQualification: Its evidential contribution depends on comparisons with natural mechanisms and with non-omniperfect designer hypotheses.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The underdetermination argument clearly distinguishes evidence for design from evidence for omniperfect Christian theism.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The evil-designer contrast is a specific rival test, though detailed likelihoods for natural alternatives remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The reply directly attacks the central fine-tuning-designer bridge and its connection to the motion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply grants limited evidential support and targets the precise extent to which it fails to identify the Christian God.

moves.evidenceBasis: Millican urges caution about future physics and argues that fine-tuning does not favor a morally perfect God over an equally powerful evil designer.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Divine hiddenness does not establish atheism because greater evidence of God's existence might not bring more people freely into a saving relationship with God.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Craig immediately before this uninterrupted first-person rebuttal, and the following transition remains within his speech.

components.text: Whether a loving God must supply more publicly compelling evidence of his existence.
Whether limited evidence is inconsistent with God's proposed saving purpose.

response.rationale: The reply offers a reason why greater evidence might not advance God's relational purpose, contacting hiddenness but not establishing the relevant counterfactual.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive purpose-based component but answers with a speculative possibility rather than a developed probability comparison.

precisionFindings.rationale: The possibility claim is clear and expressly qualified, but its scope over sincere nonbelievers is not carefully distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Repeated 'may well' and 'perhaps' language accurately presents the saving-relationship response as a possibility rather than a demonstrated fact.

charity.alternative: Some sincere nonbelievers would freely seek relationship with God if supplied clearer evidence.
charity.decisiveQualification: Greater propositional evidence need not guarantee a saving relationship, but it may still remove nonculpable epistemic barriers.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The compatibility response is coherent, but possibility of no added benefit does not establish the likelihood needed to neutralize hiddenness.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The key counterfactual about how people would respond to more evidence is speculative and unsupported in the selected span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially addresses the subsidiary defeater-answer bridge concerning divine hiddenness.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply addresses resistant unbelief but does not fully accommodate sincere seekers for whom additional evidence could matter.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig argues that God seeks saving relationship and may know that additional evidence would not bring more people freely into such relationship.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The narrow life-permitting range and multiple independent instances of cosmic fine-tuning remain evidence for design despite objections about probability, unsettled physics, efficiency, and cosmic scale.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly introduces the fine-tuning argument and sequentially answers the numbered objections attributed to Millican throughout the same speech.

components.text: Whether narrow life-permitting ranges remain design evidence despite uncertainty about probabilities and future physics.
Whether fine-tuning identifies an omniperfect Christian God rather than merely some designer.

response.rationale: The reply answers several technical objections to fine-tuning by emphasizing narrow ranges and multiple instances, but it does not resolve the designer-attribute gap.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the technical evidential component while leaving the decisive Christian-identification objection substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The intended defense is recoverable, but possible ranges, independence, and the aggregation of multiple instances remain partly unstable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Caution is acknowledged, yet simple range comparison does not alone establish a justified probability distribution or design likelihood.

charity.alternative: Fine-tuning probabilities are ill-defined and future physics may explain apparent parameter freedom.
charity.decisiveQualification: Observed narrowness can remain evidentially relevant, but only if the possible range and independence assumptions are justified.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The cumulative technical defense is coherent, but the probability-measure bridge and Christian-attribute gap remain material.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Narrow ranges and multiple cases are concrete supports, while independence, distributions, and rival likelihoods are underdeveloped.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly answers attacks on the central fine-tuning-designer bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes caution and probability objections but compresses their strongest measure and dependence qualifications.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig enumerates objections and responds that comparing possible ranges with exquisitely narrow life-permitting ranges supports fine-tuning.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Atheists can affirm intrinsic human worth and objective moral values without treating those values as ontologically dependent on God's existence.
moves.attributionBasis: Millican begins this moral discussion within his introduced final rebuttal, cites survey figures, and directly challenges positions he attributes to Craig.

components.text: Whether atheism precludes belief in objective moral value or intrinsic human worth.
Whether objective values ontologically depend on God's existence.

response.rationale: The reply expressly denies the assumed dependence and states that perceiving moral value need not causally or ontologically involve God.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the divine-dependence inference, though it does not provide a complete positive ontology of moral facts.

precisionFindings.rationale: The limited claim that atheists can affirm objective value without presupposing God is clear and appropriately scoped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The reply need only defeat alleged impossibility, and its modest claim that atheists can hold moral realism matches that burden.

charity.alternative: God may provide the best ontological foundation for objective value even if atheists psychologically believe in it.
charity.decisiveQualification: Psychological capacity to believe is distinct from a complete metaphysical account of why objective values obtain.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between perceiving moral value and positing God is coherent, with a bounded gap concerning ultimate ontology.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual counterexample is sufficient against impossibility, but no developed atheistic realist foundation is supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The reply directly attacks the central claim that objective morality requires divine grounding.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly defeats a belief-level exclusion but only partially addresses the stronger ontological-grounding version.

moves.evidenceBasis: Millican argues that God's existence makes no necessary difference to perceiving moral value and denies that atheism entails absence of intrinsic human worth.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: The Gospel resurrection narratives provide weak evidence for divine resurrection because they are late, dependent, partisan, discrepant, and unsupported by contemporary sources.
moves.attributionBasis: Millican expressly changes to the resurrection topic and sustains the critique until he announces that he must stop, with no speaker interruption.

components.text: Whether Gospel resurrection and passion narratives provide sufficiently reliable and independent historical evidence.
Whether discrepancies and absent contemporary corroboration weaken the claimed historical facts.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges source date, dependence, partisanship, coherence, and external corroboration, contacting the evidential basis of the resurrection inference.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly targets the reliability of the sources underlying the decisive historical premises.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reliability objection is clear, though 'late,' 'dependent,' and 'contemporary sources' require some historical qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cited limitations warrant substantial caution, but the rhetorical dismissal is stronger than the excerpt's selective examples establish.

charity.alternative: Ancient historical claims may remain credible despite partisan sources, partial dependence, and limited external corroboration.
charity.decisiveQualification: Credibility must be assessed claim by claim, including genre, transmission, independence, and expected corroboration.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The source-critical considerations coherently reduce evidential confidence without requiring that every narrative detail be false.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific discrepancies and absent corroboration are named, though dating, dependence, and representativeness are not fully documented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: This directly attacks the central history-and-experience reliability bridge at the resurrection evidence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply raises the right source-critical qualifications but occasionally treats vivid uncorroborated details as representative of the whole case.

moves.evidenceBasis: Millican cites non-coherence and the absence of contemporary corroboration for extraordinary Matthean passion details such as darkness and revived saints.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The resurrection best explains the asserted burial, empty tomb, appearances, and origin of the disciples' belief when prior naturalism does not exclude miracles in advance.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly introduces the resurrection, names Millican and skeptical scholars, and concludes the move by stating the proposed divine explanation.

components.text: Whether the core burial, empty-tomb, appearance, and belief data remain accepted despite narrative limitations.
Whether rejection of resurrection rests on source criticism or on antecedent naturalism about miracles.

response.rationale: The reply cites limited concessions by a skeptical scholar and argues that philosophical naturalism drives rejection, but it only partly answers source dependence and discrepancies.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the core-data and prior-probability components while leaving several direct source-critical objections unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The best-explanation thesis is clear, but 'naturalist,' 'accepts,' and the certainty assigned to each historical datum are not fully stabilized.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Some uncertainty is stated about burial, but attributing rejection chiefly to naturalism bypasses source and base-rate objections not resolved here.

charity.alternative: A historian may accept some core reports while rejecting resurrection because natural explanations and testimonial error retain higher prior probability.
charity.decisiveQualification: Low miracle priors need not be dogmatic exclusion and must be updated against the reliability and independence of the evidence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The abductive form is usable, but moving from partial core-data concessions to resurrection leaves major likelihood and source-reliability bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A named skeptical scholar's concessions provide specific support, while independence, discrepancies, and alternative likelihoods remain insufficiently answered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The reply directly defends the central Christian-identification bridge against historical-source objections.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply identifies the prior issue but materially compresses the strongest probabilistic rather than dogmatically naturalistic alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig cites concessions regarding burial, appearances, and disciples' belief and attributes continued rejection of resurrection to philosophical naturalism.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Religious experiences and resurrection reports require psychological and natural investigation because comparable supernatural claims arise in mutually incompatible traditions.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Millican for his closing statement, and he explicitly identifies religious experience before connecting it to resurrection testimony and rival claims.

components.text: Whether resurrection reports and experiences can plausibly arise through natural psychological mechanisms.
Whether immediate religious experience is sufficiently reliable to constitute knowledge.
Whether the disciples' reported experiences discriminate resurrection from natural psychological explanations.

response.rationale: The reply directly proposes psychological investigation and cross-religious comparison as alternatives to treating experience or testimony as self-authenticating.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts both experiential reliability and the natural-generation component of resurrection reports.

precisionFindings.rationale: The methodological recommendation is clear, but calling religious experience generally 'extremely unreliable' has an overbroad scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Natural psychological inquiry is clearly relevant, while the sweeping reliability judgment exceeds the particular comparative examples shown.

charity.alternative: Some religious experiences may be veridical even though incompatible or naturally caused experiences also occur.
charity.decisiveQualification: A natural mechanism's availability does not by itself explain every case, but it changes the required discrimination and reliability evidence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from comparable incompatible experiences to a need for psychological discrimination is coherent and appropriately methodological.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Cross-tradition variation provides representative support, though no specific experimental findings or base rates are developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central history-and-experience reliability burden across both resurrection and religious experience.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply does not claim that mere causal possibility settles every case and correctly emphasizes comparative empirical testing.

moves.evidenceBasis: Millican argues that comparable religious experiences require experimental-psychological inquiry into how likely the evidence is to arise naturally.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: The world's evil is empirical evidence against a perfectly good God, while limited supernatural evidence would not establish an omnipotent and omniscient deity.
moves.attributionBasis: Millican announces the problem of evil, anticipates Craig's response, and carries the argument through the explicit conclusion of his closing speech.

components.text: Whether fine-tuning or limited supernatural evidence identifies a morally perfect rather than morally indifferent or evil designer.
Whether observed evil and hiddenness fit the expected world of an omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good God.

response.rationale: The move reframes evil as discriminating empirical evidence among divine hypotheses and explicitly challenges the inference to omniperfect attributes.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the decisive attribute-identification and empirical-expectation components.

precisionFindings.rationale: The likelihood question—what world to expect under an omniperfect agent—is clearly separated from generic supernatural evidence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents evil as comparative evidence rather than a deductive disproof and frames the issue through expected observations.

charity.alternative: A perfectly good God may permit evil for morally sufficient reasons unavailable to human observers.
charity.decisiveQualification: Unknown possible reasons prevent easy deduction but do not eliminate comparative evidential expectations under perfect goodness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The likelihood-based inference from divine attributes to expected worldly goodness is explicit and avoids claiming a strict contradiction.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The observed role of suffering is pertinent, though a full likelihood comparison with specific theodicies is not supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: This directly advances the central evil-hiddenness counterevidence bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move preserves a probabilistic rather than deductive argument and focuses on discrimination among candidate divine characters.

moves.evidenceBasis: Millican asks what world an omnipotent, omniscient agent would create and argues that goodness is the crucial empirical discriminator among divine hypotheses.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Natural evil may help maximize freely formed relationships with God, while most animals may experience pain without the higher-order awareness characteristic of human suffering.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator's question concerns Craig's theistic position, and the Christian first-person answer is continuous until Millican begins his response.

components.text: Whether natural and animal suffering is inconsistent or evidentially surprising under a perfectly good God.
Whether natural conditions can serve a saving relational purpose rather than merely generating religious belief.

response.rationale: The reply offers two answers—salvific purpose and reduced animal awareness—but the empirical animal-consciousness claim and the optimization claim remain under-supported.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive suffering component but supplies speculative and empirically vulnerable explanations rather than a complete answer.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between pain and awareness of pain is evaluation-obscuring, and its restriction to higher primates is stated too broadly.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical claim that most animals are literally unaware of pain is radically stronger than the selected support and ordinary evidential caution permit.

charity.alternative: Animal pain and behavior plausibly involve conscious suffering across many vertebrate species.
charity.decisiveQualification: Higher-order self-reflection is not obviously required for phenomenally conscious pain or morally relevant suffering.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The salvific-purpose possibility is coherent, but the pain-without-awareness distinction and its moral consequence contain substantial unsupported conditionals.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The neurological assertion about frontal cortex and broad animal unawareness is selective and inadequately supported for the categorical conclusion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially addresses the subsidiary defeater-answer bridge concerning natural and animal evil.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response depends on weakening animal suffering by imposing an undefended higher-order-awareness requirement.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig claims higher-order awareness is confined to higher primates and humans and argues that other animals feel pain without awareness of being in pain.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: A God who determines nature's rules could reveal himself clearly without suffering, yet sincere rational inquiry can still terminate in justified unbelief.
moves.attributionBasis: Millican explicitly discusses Craig's familiar treatment of evil and narrates his own inquiry until the moderator introduces a new question.

components.text: Whether God must use suffering to maximize freely formed saving relationships when God determines nature's rules.
Whether sincere, rational inquiry can end in nonbelief despite a perfectly loving God's desire for relationship.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges both the necessity of suffering under divine rule-setting and the assumption that nonbelief reflects failure to examine available evidence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive purpose and sincere-nonbelief components, though its dismissal is rhetorically stronger than its development.

precisionFindings.rationale: The rule-setting objection and the claim about sincere rational unbelief are distinctly and clearly recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The counterexample from sincere inquiry is appropriately personal and qualified, though 'absolutely absurd' overstates the developed warrant.

charity.alternative: Stable natural laws and epistemic distance may be necessary for freedom, moral formation, or saving relationship.
charity.decisiveQualification: An omnipotent rule-maker still requires an account of why comparable goods could not arise with less suffering and clearer access.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The rule-maker objection coherently shifts the burden from compatibility to comparative necessity and directly supports sincere nonbelief.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The first-person case supplies a relevant counterexample to culpable unbelief, but broader representativeness and alternative divine purposes remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central evil-hiddenness counterevidence bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply reaches the strongest purpose-based answer through the rule-setting point, while leaving some detailed freedom defenses unexamined.

moves.evidenceBasis: Millican argues that God determines nature's rules and cites his own sincere engagement as evidence that rational inquiry can terminate in unbelief.
